description: "We're a team of Ulaanbaatar high schoolers skilled in coding, AI, data analysis, and STEM, ready to build a working prototype this weekend! We are looking for UI/UX designers, storytellers, Earth scientists, and project managers to complete our team.
summary:
We made Agricola, a free, open-source website in Mongolian and English. The farmer taps any field they want in Mongolia on a map. The app then gets 20 years (2006–2025) of NASA POWER data for that place, which includes temperature, rainfall and other climate aspects. It analyzes statistics from the SMAP report and data to produce complete soil information(soil moisture, type,nutritional data eg.)

From this data, it calculates the growing conditions for that field, including the number of frost-free days, how warm the summer gets, how much rain falls and how often heat stress hits during flowering. Based on the results, Agricola rates 10 crops for that specific field and ranks 8 crop rotation plans. The farmer also chooses what matters most to them, such as soil health, animal feed, income or saving water, and the rankings adjust to match. The map also shows NASA satellite layers for plant greenness (MODIS) and soil moisture (SMAP).

This is important because over 75% of Mongolia’s farmland is planted with wheat, often on the same field every year. The soil is weak and easily eroded, and the growing season is short. Agricola shows farmers better options for their own land, explains the reasons behind each recommendation, and is clear about the limits of what it can predict. It is a tool that helps them to decide and give them a chance to become more efficient.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO?

Agricola helps Mongolian farmers decide what to plant. It gets 20 years of NASA climate data for any place in Mongolia and turns it into simple farm facts: frost-free days, summer warmth, rain, heat during flowering, late and early frost, and soil wetness throughout the whole year.

Using these facts, the app rates 10 crops as good, risky or poor, and explains why. The crops are wheat, barley, oats, potato, rapeseed, pea, buckwheat, alfalfa, sea buckthorn and vegetables. It also ranks 8 crop rotation plans and compares them with what the farmer grows now. For each plan, a 12-month field calendar shows the growing months, the bare-soil months, and when there is a risk of frost or heat.

The map can also show NASA satellite layers for plant greenness (MODIS NDVI) and soil moisture (SMAP). The app opens in Mongolian, and one tap switches it to English.

HOW DOES IT WORK?

First, the farmer chooses a place. They can tap the map, use their phone’s location, or search for a province, district or village. The app checks that the place is farmland, not a lake or a town.

Next, the app asks the NASA POWER API for daily temperature, rain and soil wetness from 2006 to 2025. It turns this daily data into yearly numbers, like frost-free days and summer rain. Then it compares the last 10 years with what each crop needs, and gives each crop a rating.

To rank the rotation plans, each plan’s score comes 60% from its average crop score and 40% from its weakest crop. The farmer’s chosen priority (soil health, animal feed, income or saving water) then changes the order. Finally, the app compares 2021–2025 with 2006–2015, so farmers can see how the climate is changing.

DID WE CHECK THE DATA?

Yes. We compared NASA POWER with weather stations in 5 places(remotely). In 4 of the 5 places, rain was within about 20% and July temperature was within 1°C. For example, in Darkhan, NASA gave 310 mm of rain per year and the station gave 299 mm. In Ulaangom, the NASA data also covers nearby mountains, so the app warns users that results there are less exact.

Year by year the statistics from the NASA POWER and other external sources could be updated in live in the future. The prototype tool only focuses on the previous data to predict the current situation of the soil of the area selected while weather and climate patterns are updated in live.

BENEFITS

Farmers get clear advice in their own language, with reasons, not just a score. The rotation plans with peas, alfalfa and other crops protect the soil better than growing wheat every year. Some plans also grow animal feed, like alfalfa and oats, which helps herders too. The app is free, needs no login, and works on any sort of devices.

WHAT DO WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

Soon, we want to test Agricola with farmers and farm experts in Darkhan, Selenge and Bulgan, and improve the crop numbers with their help. Later, we hope it becomes a free tool for the whole country that helps Mongolia grow more kinds of crops and adapt to climate change. The scope of the prototype is local while our vision is beyond the global possibilities.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE?

Agricola turns global NASA data into a simple farm calendar for one place, in Mongolian. It does not give one “best” answer. Instead, the farmer chooses what matters most to them, and the app compares every plan with what they grow now. Some similar tools do not offer map selection, statistic analysis and comparison to give the absolute best suggestion to user. It does not force them to change what they are capable of, it gives them a perspective of how things work and that makes it creative.

WHAT DID WE THINK ABOUT?

We wanted the app to be honest. NASA data covers an area of about 50 km, so it cannot show the conditions of one small field. Soil type, prices and seeds are not included either, and the app says this clearly.

We also thought about farmers in rural areas. The app works on cheap phones, opens in Mongolian, and uses less animation if the phone asks for it. If an online service stops working, the app uses saved backup data and labels it as an estimate.
Farmers who sells their produced crops mostly have a working network or a connection as it is required for communication and economical purposes.

TOOLS WE USED

We built Agricola with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map. The data comes from the NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS, OpenStreetMap (Overpass and Nominatim) and Natural Earth. The app is hosted on GitHub Pages and Vercel.
